title: RBI Excludes Loans Against Fresh NRI Deposits From Priority Sector Lending Targets
excerpt: The central bank's latest move removes a key regulatory friction for banks lending against FCNR(B) and NRE deposits, building on a series of measures that have attracted over $32 billion in NRI inflows since June.
body:
• The RBI has excluded loans extended against fresh FCNR(B) and NRE deposits from banks' priority sector lending (PSL) calculations, removing a key disincentive for banks to lend against NRI deposits.
  • The move builds on a series of measures since June 2026 — including CRR/SLR exemptions, interest rate ceiling removal, and concessional forex swaps — that have collectively attracted over $32 billion in NRI deposits.
  • By freeing banks from PSL obligations on these advances, the RBI is making it more profitable for lenders to deploy NRI capital into commercial lending rather than directed sectors.
  • The decision mirrors a 2013 playbook when the RBI used identical exemptions during a rupee crisis, and signals the central bank's continued concern over forex stability amid the West Asia conflict.

The Reserve Bank of India has excluded loans extended against fresh Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR(B), and Non-Resident External (NRE) deposits from the calculation of banks' priority sector lending targets, according to an RBI circular issued on Thursday. The decision removes a significant regulatory friction that had been discouraging banks from lending against the surge of NRI deposits flowing into the system.

What Changes for Banks

Under India's banking regulations, commercial banks are required to direct 40% of their adjusted net bank credit toward priority sectors — agriculture, micro and small enterprises, education, and housing. Loans that count toward this adjusted net bank credit effectively dilute the denominator, making it harder for banks to meet their targets.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=pnWvC-QUVh8

By excluding advances against qualifying FCNR(B) and NRE deposits from this calculation, the RBI has ensured that banks can lend against NRI deposits without worrying about the impact on their PSL compliance ratios. This makes such lending commercially more attractive and removes a disincentive that had been limiting how aggressively banks deployed incoming NRI capital.

Part of a Broader NRI Deposit Push

The PSL exclusion is the latest in a series of measures the RBI has rolled out since June 2026 to attract foreign capital and stabilize the rupee amid the ongoing West Asia conflict. On June 5, the central bank announced it would bear the full hedging cost for banks raising fresh three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits through September 30. On June 17, it temporarily removed the interest rate ceiling on both FCNR(B) and NRE deposits, allowing banks to offer more competitive rates. It also exempted fresh NRE term deposits of three years or more from cash reserve ratio (CRR) and statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) requirements.

The combined impact has been substantial. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra noted in late July that banks had mobilized nearly $32 billion since June 8, with the bulk coming through the FCNR(B) route. SBI economists have projected total FCNR(B) inflows could reach $40-45 billion by the time the temporary measures expire.

"Beginning June 8th till date, banks have mobilised almost $32 billion, with most of it coming through FCNR (B) deposits."

— Sanjay Malhotra, RBI Governor

Small Banks Compete for NRI Deposits

The RBI's incentive structure has triggered a deposit-rate war, particularly among smaller lenders. Equitas Small Finance Bank raised its FCNR(B) deposit rate to 7.52%, while AU Small Finance Bank moved to 7.40% — about 150 basis points above rates offered by large banks like State Bank of India and HDFC Bank, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. Tamilnad Mercantile Bank also raised its rates to 7.25%.

Smaller banks face a structural disadvantage: they lack overseas branches or a presence in GIFT City, making it harder to offer leverage-based products to NRI clients. Instead, they are compensating with higher interest rates and negotiating with foreign banks to offer leverage arrangements backed by standby letters of credit.

A Familiar Playbook

The current approach closely mirrors the RBI's response during the 2013 rupee crisis, when the central bank issued a near-identical circular excluding advances against incremental FCNR(B) and NRE deposits from the adjusted bank credit calculation for priority sector lending. That episode saw banks mobilize over $34 billion in FCNR(B) deposits over a few months, helping stabilize the rupee after it had fallen past 68 to the dollar.

The current measures were triggered by rupee pressure stemming from the U.S.-Iran conflict and elevated oil prices. With Brent crude trading near $90 and renewed fighting around the Strait of Hormuz threatening further disruption, the RBI appears focused on building a forex buffer through stable, long-term NRI deposit inflows rather than relying on volatile portfolio flows.

What It Means for NRIs

For NRI depositors, the regulatory changes mean banks have every incentive to offer attractive rates and flexible lending terms on FCNR(B) and NRE deposits — at least until the September 30 deadline. The combination of uncapped interest rates, CRR/SLR exemptions, and now PSL exclusion creates arguably the most favorable environment for NRI deposits in over a decade. Depositors earning 7-7.5% on dollar-denominated FCNR(B) deposits are locking in returns well above comparable U.S. bank deposits, with the added benefit of repatriation flexibility.

The window, however, is temporary. Unless the RBI extends its measures beyond September 30, banks may scale back their aggressive pricing once the deadline passes.
